title: Attributes the compiler and CLR actually honor
hook: Attributes are not comments. Some are baked into IL by the compiler; others wait for reflection or a generator. Interviews fail when you treat `[Obsolete]` like a sticky note.

sections.heading: Compiler-interpreted versus user data
sections.prose: An attribute is a type derived from `System.Attribute`, applied with `[Name]` or `[assembly: Name]`. The compiler already understands a set of them: `Obsolete`, `Conditional`, `CallerMemberName`, `CallerFilePath`, `CallerLineNumber`, `CallerArgumentExpression`, `Experimental` (C# 12), `SkipLocalsInit`, and others listed in the language reference. Those change warnings, emitted IL, or which methods exist under `#define`. Your `[AuthScheme("lti")]` on a token validator is inert until an analyzer, generator, or `GetCustomAttributes` reads it. `AttributeUsage` on the attribute class restricts targets (`Method`, `Class`, `Assembly`, …) and whether it is `AllowMultiple`. Attribute constructors run when reflection instantiates them — not when the annotated method runs.

snippets.label: Obsolete versus a custom marker
snippets.explanation: Obsolete with error: true is a compiler error for callers. AuthSchemeAttribute is metadata for a generator or a one-time scan — the CLR will not enforce it.

sections.heading: Caller information is compile-time
sections.prose: Caller-info attributes decorate optional parameters. The compiler substitutes the call site: member name, source path at compile time, line number, or the argument expression as text (`CallerArgumentExpression`). That is not `Environment.StackTrace`. Obfuscation does not strip these literals. Callers may still pass the optional arguments and lie. `CallerMemberName` is the reason `OnPropertyChanged()` without a string survives rename. `CallerArgumentExpression` is how a guard can say `func is not null` failed instead of a generic “argument invalid.” C# 14 `nameof` also accepts unbound generic types (`nameof(List<>)` is `"List"`), which is a language change, not an attribute — keep them distinct in an interview.

snippets.label: Guard with CallerArgumentExpression
snippets.explanation: The compiler injects the text `body is not null`. A runtime stack walk would not give you that expression.

sections.heading: Assembly-level attributes
sections.prose: Global attributes use the `assembly` or `module` target and must appear after usings and before type declarations. SDK-style projects no longer generate a large `AssemblyInfo.cs`; version and informational attributes often live in the csproj (`<Version>`, `<Description>`). You still write `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo(...)]` and `[assembly: Experimental("MyLib.Preview")]` in source when the compiler must see them. Multiple files in one compilation may all contribute assembly attributes. Do not sprinkle `[assembly:]` inside a namespace — that is a compile error. Treat assembly attributes as the manifest of policy: friends, experimental surface, COM visibility — not a dumping ground for every constant.

interviewTakeaways: Obsolete and Experimental change compilation; custom attributes are data until something reads them.
Caller-info values are IL literals on omitted optional arguments, not a stack walk.
Assembly-level attributes belong after usings; SDK projects often map version info through the csproj instead of AssemblyInfo.cs.
commonPitfalls: Applying caller-info attributes to required parameters — they only affect omitted optional arguments.
Expecting GetCustomAttribute to return the same instance twice; each call constructs a new object.
Using [assembly:] inside a namespace or after a type declaration.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS/JS decorators wrap values at runtime (or emit metadata if enabled). C# attributes are stored in assembly metadata and may never run unless reflection or the compiler interprets them.
